intro.title: How to apologise for real
paragraphs: You missed an event that mattered to your friend, and you didn’t warn them either. The hurt is understandable. You want to make up without arguing or making excuses.
Choose what to say. If an answer doesn’t work, you stay where you are, see the reaction and understand why.
intro.note: The other person’s styles are patterns of behaviour, not types of people: the same person acts differently on different days. Real people react differently, so this is practice with wording, not a prediction.
intro.disclaimer: A learning simulation. The material draws on well-known communication methods (sources are given at each step), but it has not yet been reviewed by a psychologist.

variants.name: Hurt and quiet
variants.desc: Says little, holds feelings back, answers briefly.

variants.name: Angry and blaming
variants.desc: Speaks sharply, reproaches and expects a real acknowledgement.

nodes.narr: A café. On Saturday you weren’t at your friend’s exhibition, and you didn’t warn them. Today you’ve met to talk.

options.text: I want to apologise for Saturday. I wasn’t at your exhibition, and you didn’t hear a word from me.
options.why: An effective apology names the specific action and takes responsibility, with no “but” and no excuses.

evasive.say: Hm. Good that you said it. Go on.

options.text: Well, sorry, it just happened.
options.why: “It just happened” removes responsibility and sounds like a brush-off. The person hears that you didn’t understand what happened.

evasive.say: So that’s the apology?

options.text: Let’s not make a drama out of this.
options.why: Dismissing someone’s feelings turns an attempt to make up into a new hurt.

direct.say: To you it’s drama, to me it was an important day.

evasive.say: It mattered to me, and to you it’s drama?

options.text: I had so much going on, you know how everything piled up.
options.why: An excuse instead of responsibility tells the person “your hurt is just circumstances”. Explanations fit later, and briefly.

evasive.say: It wasn’t easy for me either, but I found the time.

tech.name: A specific admission
tech.src: Lewicki, Polin & Lount, Negotiation and Conflict Management Research, 2016
tech.text: An effective apology names exactly what happened and admits responsibility without excuses.

nodes.hint: How to start an apology so it sounds real?

evasive.say: Well, I’m listening. What is it this time?

nodes.narr: Your friend starts talking about how it was for them.

options.text: Tell me how it was for you. I’m listening.
options.why: Inviting them to talk about their feelings shows you care about understanding the consequences. Listening is part of apologising.

direct.say: Well… I came and saw an empty spot. It hurt.

evasive.say: OK. It was lonely, to be honest.

options.text: Yes, but you had other guests.
options.why: The word “but” erases the admission: the apology turns into an argument about whether the hurt is justified.

direct.say: So what? I was waiting for you.

evasive.say: It’s not about the others. It’s about you.

options.text: I’ve already apologised.
options.why: A formal tone shows you want to close the subject. The person needs to be heard, not to get a checkmark.

evasive.say: You sound like you’re in a business meeting.

options.text: You could have reminded me in advance.
options.why: Shifting the blame brings you back to arguing: the responsibility for missing it is yours.

direct.say: Seriously? I was supposed to remind you?

evasive.say: So it’s my fault too?

tech.name: Hear the consequences
tech.text: Let the person speak without objections: understand what the event meant to them.

nodes.hint: What will help you understand how it was for them?

direct.say: I waited. I kept asking everyone where you were.

evasive.say: Do you even understand what it meant to me?

nodes.narr: Your friend is sharing feelings. Now it’s important not to argue.

options.text: You felt hurt and lonely in that moment. I understand.
options.why: Reflecting a feeling shows you heard the person. You don’t have to agree with everything: it’s enough to name what they’re going through.

direct.say: Yes. Exactly. It matters to me that you hear that.

evasive.say: Well… yes. That’s how it was.

options.text: Don’t exaggerate.
options.why: This is dismissive: the person is already vulnerable, and you’re telling them their feelings are too strong.

evasive.say: Oh, I see. So I imagined it?

options.text: You forget things sometimes too.
options.why: A counter-complaint shifts attention to you. Anything about their part can be discussed another time.

direct.say: We’re not talking about me right now.

evasive.say: That’s not what I came here to talk about.

options.text: Fine, fine, it’s all my fault.
options.why: Self-blame forces your friend to comfort you and moves away from their feelings. Responsibility should be precise, not loud.

evasive.say: Don’t play the victim.

tech.name: Reflecting feelings
tech.text: Name the other person’s feelings in your own words, without judging or arguing.

nodes.hint: How to show you heard their feelings?

direct.say: It really hurt. And I was a bit embarrassed that I’d told everyone you’d come.

evasive.say: I felt awful. I stood there like an idiot.

options.text: I want to make it right: I’ll come on Sunday to see the work, and for the next exhibition I’ll set a reminder in advance.
options.why: A specific offer to make things right is an important part of an apology: words are backed by an action you will really do.

direct.say: Sunday… yes, come. I’d like that.

evasive.say: OK. Come on Sunday.

options.text: Tell me, what do you need to feel better?
options.why: The question is fair, but it hands your friend the job of inventing how to forgive you. Stronger: suggest your own option and ask if it works.

direct.say: Hm. Well… come see the work, I guess.

evasive.say: I don’t know. Think of something.

options.text: Well, what’s done is done.
options.why: This phrase closes off any repair: the person hears that you don’t care.

evasive.say: Fine. Then there’s nothing to talk about.

options.text: Let me buy you something to make up for it.
options.why: A gift instead of attention reads as a pay-off: you’re paying for forgiveness instead of fixing what you did.

evasive.say: You think this can be bought?

tech.name: An offer to make it right
tech.src: Lewicki, Polin & Lount, Negotiation and Conflict Management Research, 2016
tech.text: A specific action that restores trust: not a promise of “never again”, but a clear step.

nodes.hint: What exactly will you do to make it right?

evasive.say: So what now, an apology and that’s it?

nodes.narr: The conversation is coming to an end. It’s important to finish honestly.

options.text: Thanks for the talk. I’ll come on Sunday as we agreed, and I’ll text you the day before.
options.why: Confirming the agreement with a specific step restores trust: the words are backed by a date.

evasive.say: OK. See you on Sunday.

options.text: Well, that’s nice, friends again?
options.why: Asking “friends again?” demands immediate forgiveness. The person needs time, and they have every right to it.

evasive.say: Don’t rush me.

options.text: It will never happen again, I swear!
options.why: A big promise is easy to break, and a broken promise costs more. A specific step is more reliable than vows.

direct.say: I’ve heard promises like that before.

evasive.say: Don’t swear. Just do it.

options.text: Well, OK, I have to go.
options.why: Leaving abruptly after a hard conversation makes it feel like it didn’t matter that much to you.

evasive.say: Off you go.

tech.name: Confirm the agreement
tech.text: End the conversation with a specific promise: when and what exactly you’ll do.

nodes.hint: How to finish in a way that restores trust?

direct.say: Good. It mattered to me to hear that.

evasive.say: OK. We’ll see how it goes.
OK. Till Sunday.

finale.title: An apology that makes things lighter
finale.lead: Your friend was heard, responsibility was named, and a step to repair was taken. Here’s what it relied on:
carry: Naming the specific thing, not “it just happened”.
Listening and naming feelings instead of defending yourself.
Offering an action you will do, and keeping your word.
finale.prompt: How would your apology sound in a real situation? Write down your version to come back to before the meeting.
